title: No five on a sphere in a 12 × 12 × 12 grid
description: Find more points in the 12 × 12 × 12 grid than the best known set, with no 5 of them on one sphere or one plane. A short Python program checks any set in a few seconds at most.
objective: Find a set of points in the 12 x 12 x 12 grid such that no 5 of them lie on one sphere or one plane. The score is the number of points; a larger set gives a better lower bound on C(12).

bestKnown.by: AlphaEvolve, run and reported by Bogdan Georgiev, Javier Gómez-Serrano, Terence Tao, Adam Zsolt Wagner
bestKnown.quote: We also got the new lower bounds $C_{\ref{nosphere}}(11) \geq 31$ and $C_{\ref{nosphere}}(12) \geq 33$.
bestKnown.note: arXiv 2511.02864v3 TeX source, appendix.tex line 1973, section 'The no 5 on a sphere problem'. The 33 points are published in the problem 60 notebook (best_known.json).

objectFormat: A JSON object {"n": 12, "points": [[x, y, z], ...]} where every coordinate is an integer from 0 to 11 (the grid {1..12}^3 shifted by -1, as the source publishes its construction; a shift maps spheres to spheres and planes to planes). Points must be distinct; at most 48 points (more than 4n points always put 5 on one plane z = c). No other keys: an accepted object is shown publicly. At most 20,000 bytes as the result file carries it.
shows: That this one set of points has no 5 points on a common sphere or plane and has the stated number of points, so C(12) is at least that number. With more points than the best known set, it is better than the value in the named source as of the date shown.
notCovered: A pass shows only that this one finite set has no 5 points on a common sphere or plane and has the stated size, so C(12) is at least that size. It does not give the exact value of C(12), says nothing about other n or about the asymptotic bounds, does not show the set is optimal, and does not show who found it or how.
alsoBelongsAt: The AlphaEvolve repository of problems, problem 60 (its README says: "Comments are most welcome - please feel free to contact the repository owners or send a pull request.")
effort: Hours of search at least, and it may not succeed: in a one-hour attempt an AI app with local search did not reach the best known value.
resultLine: Result: an accepted run's set passed this task's checker on Papex's runner and had more points than the best known set at that time, so C(12) is at least its size. It says nothing about the largest possible set, and it is not peer review.
requirements: Python 3.9 or later and git. An AI app with a terminal and the Papex connection, or your own code, to search. No special hardware.
checkedHow: tasks/no-five-on-a-sphere-12/checker.py (Python, standard library only) tests that the points are distinct and inside the grid, then computes for every 5 of them, in exact integers, the 5 × 5 determinant with rows (x, y, z, x² + y² + z², 1), which is zero exactly when the five lie on one sphere or plane. Papex's runner runs the same checker again on the object in the result file and compares the number of points with the best known value on Papex at that moment.

create.title: The no 5 on a sphere problem
create.question: How many points can be chosen from the n × n × n grid so that no 5 of them lie on one sphere or one plane?
create.summary: Problem 60 of the AlphaEvolve repository of problems (Georgiev, Gómez-Serrano, Tao and Wagner, 2025). C(n) is the size of the largest subset of the n × n × n grid with no 5 points on a sphere or a plane. It is known that C(n) ≤ 4n; the source asks for upper and lower bounds on C(n) that are as strong as possible.

sources.fact: The problem as its source states it
sources.quote: For $n$ a natural number, let $C(n)$ denote the size of the largest subset of $[n]^3 = \{1,\dots,n\}^3$ such that no 5 points lie on a sphere or a plane. Obtain upper and lower bounds for $C(n)$ that are as strong as possible.
We also got the new lower bounds $C_{\ref{nosphere}}(11) \geq 31$ and $C_{\ref{nosphere}}(12) \geq 33$.

sources.fact: The general bounds: at most 4n, at least n^(3/4 - o(1))
The published 33-point set, copied into best_known.json
